coupled_spring_potential.text: The Lean theorem writes out the polynomial in a let expression and states IsLocalMin at the zero vector. That means U(0) ≤ U(x) on a neighbourhood. The global inequality has its own passage and proof.

second_derivative_test_analyticAt.text: Lean takes a finite-dimensional real inner product space, analyticity and zero gradient at the point, and PosDef of the map h ↦ D²f(a)[h,h]. Its conclusion is IsLocalMin, with a weak inequality on a neighbourhood.

couplingPotential_analyticAt.text: The point z is arbitrary in EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2). Lean proves analyticity at each such point.

couplingPotential_hasFDerivAt.text: Lean defines the continuous linear map as (2x₀+x₁) times the first coordinate projection plus (x₀+2x₁) times the second. Applying that map to h gives the displayed derivative.

couplingPotential_gradient_zero.text: Lean states gradient couplingPotential !₂[0, 0] = 0. The vector !₂[0, 0] is the origin of the Euclidean plane.

couplingPotential_iteratedFDeriv_two.text: Lean evaluates the second derivative on two arbitrary vectors. The four coefficients of the resulting bilinear expression give the entries of K, independent of the base point z.

couplingPotential_posDef.text: Lean asserts positivity of the Hessian quadratic map at the origin on nonzero vectors. The lower bound by ‖h‖² in the next sentence follows from the displayed squares.

isLocalMin_of_posDef_of_littleo.text: The page's argument needs the Taylor estimate, a zero gradient and a positive definite second derivative. The Lean statement also assumes ContDiffAt ℝ ⊤ f x₀, so it says less than the argument gives. Its proof obtains the lower bound from coercive_of_posdef and again from coercive_of_posdef_of_contdiff, and only the second uses the extra hypothesis. The supplementary Lean proof reaches the same conclusion without it.

polarBilin_iteratedFDerivQuadraticMap.text: The full polar form sums the second derivative on the ordered pairs (u,v) and (v,u). Recovering the Hessian off the diagonal requires halving the sum and using symmetry.
